title: Magies Student Reward & Evolution System

contributors.contribution: Created the character artwork used for the Magies and their evolution stages.
Rigged and animated the Magies in Spine across their evolution and expression states.
Worked with Jamie on the overall Magies game concept and reviewed/approved the finished character progression with the team.

description: I co-designed and implemented Magies, a persistent student reward system used across most Essential Skills programs. Students earned crystals by scoring 80% or higher on learning activities, then spent them in the Magie Shop to unlock more than 100 animated creatures and evolve them from Egg to Baby, Teen, and Adult stages. I also built the persistence, reward integration, asset-processing pipeline, and internal QA tools used to manage the full production system.

sections.title: Reward System Design
paragraphs: Magies was designed as a persistent reward system tied directly to student mastery rather than as an unrelated mini-game.
I worked with my boss on the overall game concept and designed the progression and reward economy that connected student performance to collection and evolution.

sections.title: Mastery-Based Crystal Economy
paragraphs: Students earned one crystal whenever they scored 80% or higher on an activity or its pre-test equivalent.
Only one crystal was awarded for the completed activity, creating a simple and predictable mastery-based reward loop.

sections.title: Persistent Reward Integration
paragraphs: The reward was applied by the shared activity system when the qualifying activity was completed, even if the student was not currently looking at the Magies interface.
This allowed the reward economy to remain persistent across normal lesson activity rather than requiring students to enter a separate game mode first.

sections.title: Magie Evolution
paragraphs: Each Magie progressed through four visual stages.

sections.title: Magie Shop
paragraphs: Students spent earned crystals in the Magie Shop to unlock new Magies and additional evolution stages.
The shop turned academic progress into a long-term collection and progression loop rather than a one-time reward animation.

sections.title: Collection Across Programs
paragraphs: Each Essential Skills program could give the student another set of Magies to discover. The assignment logic avoided repeats across those program-specific sets and included rarer and epic Magies.
The exact rarity-selection algorithm is not retained strongly enough to document publicly, but rarity was part of the production collection design.

sections.title: Visit & Collection Viewing
paragraphs: Students could visit Magies they already owned to view their current evolution stage and animations.
The Visit state was primarily a collection/viewing experience rather than a separate gameplay system.

sections.title: SimpleDB Persistence
paragraphs: Student Magie ownership, progression, and reward state were stored in SimpleDB so collection progress persisted across sessions and applications.

sections.title: Part of a Broader Reward Architecture
paragraphs: Magies was one of several persistent reward models supported by the platform. Other programs could use stars, badges, trophies, or achievement-style rewards.
Some alternate reward systems reused the same underlying currency logic. For example, earned reward currency could be applied toward badges without exposing that implementation detail to the student.

sections.title: Suite Integration
paragraphs: Magies was integrated across most Essential Skills programs. Mad Minute was the main remembered exception.
Because the reward logic lived below the individual activity UI, the same progression system could work across many different learning-program and activity types.

sections.title: 100+ Production Characters
paragraphs: The final system contained more than 100 Magies, and all of them were live in production for years.
Each character had multiple evolution stages and animated expression states, creating a significant asset-management and QA problem in addition to the gameplay logic.

sections.title: Spine Animation Pipeline
paragraphs: Character animation was produced in Spine. One artist created the character artwork and another team member animated the characters, while my boss and I reviewed and approved the results.
I built the software pipeline that moved those finished animation packages from artist output into testable production assets.

sections.title: React Artist Upload Tool
paragraphs: I built a React-based upload tool so completed Spine animation packages could be submitted into the production pipeline without manually assembling all of their runtime files.

sections.title: AWS Lambda Asset Processing
paragraphs: An AWS Lambda trigger processed uploaded animation packages, reformatted them into the structure expected by the runtime and testing tools, and stored the resulting assets in Amazon S3.
This automated a repetitive part of the artist-to-production workflow and made the large number of Magies easier to manage consistently.

sections.title: Animation & Evolution QA Tool
paragraphs: I also built an internal testing tool that displayed all four evolution stages of a Magie at the same time.
The tester could cycle through the available animation and expression states for each evolution so problems could be found before the character was released.

sections.title: Production Review Workflow
paragraphs: The production flow involved artwork creation, Spine animation, upload, automated formatting, S3 storage, technical testing, and final review.
My role covered the architecture, game/reward logic, backend integration, asset pipeline, internal tooling, and final technical validation.

historicalNotes: The Magies development period is best represented as 2019–2020 because the software system and the production integration of more than 100 animated characters took substantial time.
Spine by Esoteric Software is the correct animation technology. Older profile references to 'Spline' are typos and should be corrected to Spine.
Jamie worked with his boss on the overall game concept and personally designed the progression/reward economy and implemented the software system.
The reward currency was described historically as both gems and crystals because the currency visually resembled gem-like crystals. Public wording should standardize on 'crystals'.
Students earned one crystal when they achieved a score of 80% or higher on an activity or pre-test equivalent.
The reward could be applied even when the student did not immediately see the Magies interface.
Evolution stages were Egg, Baby, Teen, and Adult.
Crystals were used in the Magie Shop to unlock Magies and their evolution stages.
Visit meant viewing/interacting with an already-owned Magie rather than a separate gameplay mode.
Magie ownership/progression was persisted in SimpleDB.
Each program could assign another set of Magies to a student, avoiding repeats and including rare/epic variants.
The exact rarity-selection algorithm is not confidently remembered and should not be described publicly without further evidence.
The platform supported multiple persistent reward systems including Magies, badges/trophies/achievements, and simple stars.
Some alternate reward systems reused the same underlying currency mechanism while presenting a different reward experience to the student.
Mad Minute is the main remembered program that did not use the Magies system.
The internal QA tool displayed all four evolution stages simultaneously and allowed Jamie to cycle through animation/expression states for each.
The Magies production group consisted of Jamie, his boss, one character artist, and one Spine animator.
One artist created the character images and another animated the assets in Spine.
Jamie and his boss reviewed and approved the finished character work.
Jamie built a React upload tool for completed Spine animation packages.
An AWS Lambda trigger formatted uploaded animation data into testable runtime units and stored them in S3.
Jamie used the internal testing application to verify the animation/expression states of all evolutions before release.
More than 100 Magies were live in production for years.
The original portfolio card only summarized the crystal/evolution loop and materially understated the production asset pipeline, persistence, QA tooling, and cross-suite integration.
